output.text_response:
Plan created. Mode taken: **create (first plan)** for q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Step 1 survey — facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845, Ireland (tree records Ireland; the project objective says "Pennsylvania" — a discrepancy to watch); Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (S3, death cert no. 4521)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818, Ireland — this fact has no source attached; it is an unsupported assumption in the tree
- ParentChild relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick): evidenced by S1 (1850 census — assertions a_004/a_005 for q_001), S2 (1860 census — in tree but no q_001 assertions extracted from it), S3 (death cert — in tree but no q_001 parentage assertions extracted from it)
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records): in the source list; no assertions from it anywhere
- No wife of Thomas or mother of Patrick appears anywhere in the tree — identifying the mother is the central gap

---

**Plan pl_002 — 6 items in execution order:**

- **pli_004** — census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1870, **Ancestry** (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/) — name-searchable. Patrick ~25, Thomas ~52 in 1870; the wife/mother would appear by name if still living. First opportunity to identify the mother. Search Flynn/Flinn/Flin.
- **pli_005** — probate, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1851–1930, FamilySearch — browse-only; browse image group 007936749 (412 images). S4 is in the source list with no assertions yet. A will naming Patrick as son = direct parentage evidence; a will or administration naming a wife reveals the mother.
- **pli_006** — vital_record (Thomas's marriage), Pennsylvania, 1838–1855, FamilySearch — name-searchable (Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950). No wife of Thomas is anywhere in the tree; the marriage record is the primary route to the mother's maiden name.
- **pli_007** — church, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1842–1895, FamilySearch — name-searchable (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records). RC parish registers may hold Thomas's marriage entry, a burial naming survivors, or a sibling's baptism naming both parents. Search Flynn/Flinn/Flin.
- **pli_008** — church (image browse), Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1842–1895, FamilySearch — browse-only fallback for pli_007; image group 007936751 (187 images). Browse page by page if pli_007 yields nothing.
- **pli_009** — vital_record (Patrick's own marriage), Pennsylvania, 1865–1908, FamilySearch — name-searchable. Patrick's marriage license or certificate would name his parents, providing direct corroboration of both father and mother.

Fallback: if pli_007 (church name search) yields nothing, execute pli_008 (browse image group 007936751).

Total: 6 searches (5 primary, 1 fallback triggered only if pli_007 is empty).

---

**Summary:** The plan covers the parentage question for Patrick Flynn — Thomas Flynn is already in the tree as candidate father but with no source for his own birth and no mother identified anywhere. The first search is the **1870 census on Ancestry** (pli_004), as requested: in 1870, Patrick would be ~25 and Thomas ~52, and if Thomas's wife was still living she would appear by name in the household — the clearest single step toward identifying the mother. The plan then moves to Thomas's probate records (his will naming Patrick as son is the strongest parentage evidence; the will or inventory may also name his wife), Thomas's marriage record in Pennsylvania civil marriages (the mother's maiden name directly), Catholic parish registers in Schuylkill County, and finally Patrick's own marriage record, which commonly names both parents on the license.

**Next step:** Run the Ancestry 1870 census search first (pli_004) via search-external-sites, then the FamilySearch searches in order via search-records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

No wife of Thomas Flynn or mother of Patrick is recorded anywhere in the project tree. Thomas's marriage record is the primary document to supply the mother's maiden name — the central gap in this parentage question. With Patrick born ~1845, the marriage likely occurred between 1838 and the mid-1840s. FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' (collection 1571957) is name-searchable. Search under 'Thomas Flynn' and spelling variants. Note the limit: the couple's marriage confirms they wed and its date corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father by establishing the couple before 1845, but it does not by itself prove Patrick is their child — a record placing Patrick with the parents (as in the census) remains needed alongside it. FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415). Search under 'Flynn,' 'Flinn,' and 'Flin.' Note: Patrick's birth is recorded as Ireland (~1845), so a Schuylkill baptism for him would only appear if the family arrived before 1845 or a local re-registration occurred — the baptism abroad is outside this plan's scope.

Volume search returned image group 007936751 (Schuylkill County church records, 1842-1895, 187 images, bilingual English/German), which is browse-only (personCount 0). If the name-searchable collection in pli_004 yields no Flynn results, browse this image group page by page for sacramental entries involving the Flynn or Flinn family.

FAN-cluster item: Patrick Flynn's own marriage record would name his parents, either corroborating or adding to what census and probate searches establish. Patrick (b. ~1845, d. 1908-03-12) would have married between roughly 1865 and 1900. FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950' (collection 1921317) is name-searchable (personCount 1,048,378) and covers the later part of this window; also search 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' (collection 1571957) for earlier years. This item bears on the parentage question by potentially naming both Patrick's father and mother on the marriage license or certificate as the groom's parents.

A woman enumerated with them is likely Patrick's mother; the 1860 census does not record relationships explicitly, but household order and age provide strong context. The 1880 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) was the first federal census to record every person's relationship to the head of household. Thomas Flynn (~62) or Patrick Flynn (~35) would appear; a woman listed as Thomas's 'wife' is direct evidence of her identity as Patrick's mother. The 1900 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) uniquely records the birthplace of each enumerated person's father and mother. Irish immigrants in Schuylkill County's anthracite coal region were predominantly Roman Catholic; the locality guide notes that sacramental registers are held at the parish and diocese, not the county. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

---

### What You Need to Do — 5 Steps in Order

All records are at **Archion** (a paid German church-archive site) because Baiersbronn's registers are not on FamilySearch. Start at the Baiersbronn parish page:
**https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn**

---

**pli_001 — Württemberg Familienregister** *(highest yield — do this first)*
Browse the "S" section of the Familienregister for **Seeger / Seger / Säger**. This Württemberg-specific record organises the whole family unit in one entry — father, mother (with maiden name), and all children with dates. Scope: 1808–1880.

**pli_002 — Baptism Register, ~1840–1846**
Browse baptisms in the window around 1843 for a Katharina Seeger entry. It will name her father directly (and often her mother). Cross-checks item 1.

**pli_003 — Burial Register, 1843–1880** *(FAN/relatives search)*
Browse Seeger burials. A parent who died in Baiersbronn would have an entry giving age, occupation, and surviving spouse — independent evidence of parentage.

**pli_004 — Marriage Register, 1825–1845**
Once you have the parents' names from items 1–2, find their marriage. This confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name.

**pli_005 — Katharina's Own Marriage or Death Record, 1858–1880**
If Katharina married or died in the Freudenstadt district, that record names her parents directly — no prior knowledge of their identity needed. Pre-1870 church records are on Archion; post-1870 civil records are at the **Landesarchiv Baden-Württemberg** (may require a written request).

---

**Total scope: 5 browse-only image searches** — items 1–4 on Archion, item 5 split between Archion and the Landesarchiv. Work through them in order; the Familienregister (item 1) alone may answer the question in one browse session. Let me know if you'd like help capturing or uploading a page from Archion.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) last appears in the tree in the 1860 census and likely died between ca. 1861 and ca. 1900. The proof summary (ps_001) names his probate records as the primary remaining gap. FamilySearch collection 1999196 ('Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994') is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 covers Schuylkill County probate 1851-1930 (412 images). A will naming Patrick Flynn as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. S4 in the project tree already records this source description; the search itself has not yet run. Per loc_001, the Schuylkill County Register of Wills has held probate records since the county's formation in 1811.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required for this parentage question: it would (a) confirm them as a married couple; (b) supply the mother's maiden name, which no tree fact or source currently provides; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth, corroborate the father-son link suggested by census co-residence alone. Patrick's birth ~1845 in Ireland indicates Thomas and his wife likely married in Ireland before emigrating, but some Irish immigrants married on arrival in Pennsylvania, making a Schuylkill County church search worthwhile before turning to Irish records. FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH ('Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records') is name-searchable and covers 1708-1985. Per loc_001, Catholic sacramental registers from Schuylkill County parishes are filmed and indexed in this collection. Search variant spellings: Flynn, Flinn, Flin. Note: the couple's marriage record proves their union but not that Patrick is their child; a household or baptism record is still needed to place Patrick with them.

Patrick Flynn (born ~1845 Ireland, died 1908 Schuylkill County) likely participated in Catholic parish life in the anthracite coal region. The timeline (t_001) shows a high gap from 1860 to 1908 with no sacramental events recorded. A marriage record, confirmation entry, or burial record filed by his parish may name his parents or the home parish in Ireland from which the family came. FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable and covers sacramental registers from Schuylkill County parishes, which were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961, per loc_001. Search variant spellings: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

Image group 007936751 is a browse-only (personCount 0) unindexed film of Schuylkill County church records, 1842-1895 (187 images, in English and German). Per loc_001, some coal-region church films are browse-only image groups that do not appear in the indexed collection. This item is the fallback for pli_008 (Patrick in parish records): if the name-searchable collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH returns nothing for Flynn/Flinn, browse this image group page by page for family entries. It also extends coverage of pli_007 (Thomas and wife's marriage) into the unindexed range.

Patrick Flynn's marriage is a distinct target from the church-records name search above: this item targets the county civil marriage register, image group 007936753 (Marriage Records, 1870-1910, browse-only, personCount 0, 94 images). Patrick was last seen in the tree in 1860; a marriage between ca. 1865 and ca. 1895 is plausible. The informants on a marriage record are the parties themselves, so any parental names stated there are primary information — the highest-quality informant available for this event. Browse for Flynn and Flinn entries across the volume. This also fills the high 1860-1908 timeline gap flagged by t_001.

FAN research: image group 007936752 (Deed Records, 1815-1900, 543 images, 22% indexed). Boundary recitals in deeds name adjoining landowners who are frequently neighbors and kin; deed witnesses and co-grantees supply additional FAN names. A deed in Thomas Flynn's name may identify relatives or community members who could corroborate the family unit or supply details the probate and church records lack. Thomas Flynn's presence in the Schuylkill County anthracite coal region from at least 1850 makes land transactions plausible. At 22% indexed, run a name search first, then browse the unindexed images for the relevant years.

Search FindAGrave for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County Catholic and community cemeteries. A tombstone inscription or burial record may name his wife, his nativity (county or parish in Ireland), or his children, providing independent contextual evidence of the family unit. Thomas was born ~1818 and was last seen alive in 1860; he likely died before 1908. If a stone names a wife or children, that is corroborating evidence for the parent-child link with Patrick. Per loc_001, Catholic cemeteries in the coal region are sometimes transcribed in FindAGrave. This is a fallback for the probate item (pli_006): if no will is found naming heirs, a cemetery record is the next-best independent source for family composition.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The tree records Michael's 1882 Schuylkill County residence unsourced. The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the closest enumeration before that date and would show where Michael was living in June 1880 — either already in Schuylkill County (meaning the move predates 1882) or in a different county or state (documenting the subsequent migration). His listed occupation would confirm or expand on the unsourced 'Miner' entry in the tree. Search variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shahan.

The tree records an unsourced 1870 Pennsylvania residence for Michael — no county is given. The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) would confirm which Pennsylvania county he was in at that time and what occupation he held, establishing his location a full decade before the Schuylkill County move. If he is outside Schuylkill County in 1870, combined with the 1880 census result, it defines the migration window precisely. Search variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shahan.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) would confirm that Michael remained in Schuylkill County after the circa-1882 move and continued in mining employment. The 1900 schedule uniquely asked how many years the enumeree had been in the United States, which — if Sheahan is an Irish immigrant surname, as seems likely — would establish when he arrived in the country and thus the timing relative to the Schuylkill County move. Search variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shahan.

The 1910 US Census (collection 1488411, name-searchable) extends the tracking of Michael's continued presence in Schuylkill County and mining occupation into the next decade. If Michael is not found in the 1900 census, the 1910 search covers the possibility he was temporarily absent or that the 1900 record is damaged or mis-indexed. The 1910 schedule asked years of current marriage and industry/employer type, which may distinguish anthracite from other mining.

Sheahan is an Irish surname, and Irish immigrants formed the core labor pool of the Schuylkill anthracite coal fields. Naturalization records for Schuylkill County (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0), covering 1849-1915) would record Michael's country and county of birth and his year of arrival in the United States — directly establishing whether the Schuylkill County move was part of an immigration journey to the coal region. These must be browsed image-by-image; loc_001 notes that some anthracite-region naturalization films are browse-only.

Pennsylvania statewide civil registration of deaths began in 1906 (per loc_001). Collection 2255317 is name-searchable. If Michael died in 1906 or later, his death certificate would state his occupation, birthplace, and often how long he had resided in Pennsylvania — directly corroborating whether he was an anthracite coal miner and where he came from before Schuylkill County. The informant's relationship to Michael affects the reliability of secondary information such as birthplace; a certificate stating a different occupation would weigh against the family tradition. Search variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shahan.

Irish coal-mining families in Schuylkill County were predominantly Roman Catholic, under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875, per loc_001). Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable and covers Schuylkill County parish registers from 1708 to 1985. A baptism, marriage, or burial entry for Michael Sheahan in a Schuylkill County parish would confirm his presence in the county and may record a birthplace or parents' origin. Volume 007936751 (browse-only (personCount 0), Church Records 1842-1895) covers the same register set for years not yet indexed and would be consulted if the indexed collection returns nothing. Search variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shahan.

Schuylkill County and regional histories published in the late 19th and early 20th centuries often contain biographical sketches of mining community residents, descriptions of individual collieries, and accounts of Irish immigrant settlement in the anthracite fields (Appendix B: local histories). As a FAN source, these may name neighbors, associates, and fellow immigrants — including Sheahan family members — who traveled together from Ireland to the Schuylkill coal region, corroborating a chain-migration pattern. No tool returned a specific address or finding-aid number for the Historical Society of Schuylkill County; the researcher should locate current contact information on the Historical Society's own website before visiting or requesting a search.

output.text_response:
**Research Plan for q_001 — "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"**

**Mode:** Create — first plan for q_001

---

## Current State

The tree records Patrick Flynn (I1) with a death of 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, PA, and lists Thomas Flynn (I2, b. ~1818, Ireland) as a possible father via the 1850 census co-enumeration. No mother for Patrick is recorded anywhere. Hypothesis h_001 (Thomas Flynn is Patrick's father) is rated "possible" and rests on a single indirect assertion.

---

## Plan pl_002 — 8 Items in Execution Order

| # | Record Type | Place | Years | Repository | Notes |
|---|-------------|-------|-------|------------|-------|
| pli_004 | **1880 Census** | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1880 | FamilySearch | First priority — explicitly records relationship to head & parents' birthplaces |
| pli_005 | **Probate records** (Thomas Flynn) | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1855–1895 | FamilySearch | Browse-only, image group 007936749 (412 images); would directly name Patrick as a son |
| pli_006 | **Church records** (indexed) | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1845–1875 | FamilySearch | Best chance to identify Patrick's mother; collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (~982K persons) |
| pli_007 | **Church records** (images) | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1842–1895 | FamilySearch | Fallback for pli_006; browse-only image group 007936751 (187 images) |
| pli_008 | **Thomas Flynn's marriage** | Pennsylvania | 1840–1865 | FamilySearch | PA Civil & Compiled Marriages; Patrick born in Ireland ~1845, so result likely nil, but worth checking |
| pli_009 | **1870 Census** | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1870 | FamilySearch | If Thomas absent, narrows probate window for pli_005 |
| pli_010 | **1900 Census** | Schuylkill Co., PA | 1900 | FamilySearch | Last census Patrick can appear in; records year of immigration |
| pli_011 | **Patrick's marriage** | Pennsylvania | 1865–1908 | FamilySearch | Some 19th-century registers name the groom's father |

*pli_007 is searched only if pli_006 returns nothing.*

---

## Why This Order

1. **1880 census first** — unlike earlier censuses, it names the relationship to the head of household and records where each person's parents were born, making it the single most efficient search.
2. **Probate next** — a will from Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as his son would be direct proof of parentage.
3. **Church records** — baptism registers name both parents, the only likely path to identifying Patrick's unknown mother.
4. **Supporting searches** — cover Thomas's marriage, the 1870 and 1900 censuses to track the family across time, and Patrick's own marriage record (which sometimes named the groom's father).

---

**Next step:** Hand to **search-records** for execution. All eight repositories are FamilySearch. Confirm before starting.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Pennsylvania had no civil birth registration before 1906 (localities entry loc_001). The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable (personCount 982,415), covering 1708-1985. Searching baptisms with surname Doyle and mother's given name Bridget or mother's maiden name Halloran within 1855-1885 — Bridget's likely child-bearing window given her birth ~1838 — should surface each child by name and date. Halloran may also appear as Hallaren or Haloran.

The 1880 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1417683) uniquely recorded each person's relationship to the head of household, making it the most reliable census for family reconstruction. A search for John or Bridget Doyle in Schuylkill County would list all children entered as 'son' or 'daughter' still at home in June 1880. Bridget (~42) would likely still have younger children at home.

The 1870 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1438024) captures the Doyle household when Bridget was ~32, covering children born in the 1860s who may have left home by 1880. Comparing the 1870 and 1880 household rosters identifies children who appear in one census but not the other — particularly older children who had established independent households by 1880.

The 1860 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1473181) is the earliest census covering the period after Bridget's likely immigration. At ~22 she may already have had a child or two; this is the gateway to the oldest Doyle children, including any who died before 1870 and so never appear in later censuses.

The 1900 US Federal Census (name-searchable, collection 1325221) asked every woman the number of children she had borne and how many were then living. Locating Bridget Halloran/Doyle (born Ireland ~1838) in 1900 — whether still as a Doyle or under a later married name — supplies a count of all children she carried to term, against which the baptismal and census evidence can be checked for completeness. Any surviving Doyle children still residing with or near her would appear in the same or adjacent households.

Children of Bridget and John Doyle who married in Schuylkill County between 1870 and 1910 would appear in the county marriage registers. A marriage entry routinely names both parties' parents, constituting direct evidence linking each child to Bridget and John Doyle. entry.rationale: Sweden, Baptisms, 1611-1920 (collection 1520594) is name-searchable with over 20 million persons. Elena married in December 1712 at an estimated age of 17-27, placing her birth circa 1685-1695. Her patronymic surname Asmundsdotter confirms her father was named Asmund. Search for Elena and all documented name variants — Elena = Helena = Ellen = Elin = Eljena, per the Sweden_Naming_Customs wiki page — with surname Asmundsdotter (also abbreviated d., dr., dtr.) in the Malmöhus area. A hit would directly supply her baptism date and her parents' names. Note: Västra Karaby's register begins 1688 (loc_002), so a birth before 1688 would leave no baptism entry in that parish's register; the national index draws from multiple parishes and may cover a nearby parish where an earlier entry survives.

The marriage of Elena Asmundsdotter and Jöns Jönsson on 29 December 1712 in Västra Karaby is recorded in the project tree as a fact with no source attached. The Västra Karaby church records (collection 1974200) are browse-only (personCount 0); image groups 004523021 and 004523018 cover this parish through 1804. Browsing the marriage register around December 1712 retrieves the original entry, which in Swedish Lutheran practice of this era routinely recorded the groom's and bride's fathers' names — the most direct potential source for naming Elena's parents. The image group 004523021 also covers Saxtorp parish in the same volumes, which may be relevant if Elena originated there.

Per Appendix B, a parentage plan requires a dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage. Elena's father was Asmund (from her patronymic); her mother's given name and maiden name are unknown. Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 (collection 1520596) is name-searchable with over 3.6 million persons. Search for a groom named Asmund in the Harjager härad or Malmöhus county area, circa 1675-1702. The date window is set to the plausible range for a couple whose daughter married in 1712 (parents' marriage approximately 15-37 years before the daughter's). This record would supply the mother's maiden name — unavailable from the patronymic — and confirm the parents as a couple. Note the limit: this record proves the couple married but does not by itself place Elena as their child; a record co-locating Elena with her parents (items 1, 4) is still required for a parentage conclusion.

Image group 004523018 covers Västra Karaby 1688-1804 and is browse-only (personCount 0), as part of collection 1974200. Swedish husförhörslängder (household examination rolls) organized each household and listed all members with their ages, updated across multiple years. Browsing pre-1712 rolls in Västra Karaby would show a household headed by Asmund and list Elena as a daughter still resident before her December 1712 marriage — directly placing her in her natal household and confirming parentage. The rolls may also record Elena's year of birth, corroborating or correcting the estimate from her marriage age. If Asmund's household is absent from Västra Karaby rolls, that narrows the parish of origin to elsewhere in the härad.

Elena's death date is unknown; she was demonstrably alive in September 1718 when her son was christened. Sweden, Burials, 1649-1920 (collection 1520597) is name-searchable with nearly 2.9 million persons. Search for Elena Asmundsdotter, or under her married household (wife of Jöns Jönsson) in Malmöhus county from 1718 onward. Swedish burial register entries of this era commonly recorded the deceased's age at death and home parish or place of origin — evidence that could supply her birthplace and narrow the birth-year window for the baptism search. This item is also required because Västra Karaby's register begins 1688 (loc_002), and Elena's birth may predate it: if no baptism entry survives, a burial entry stating her age or origin becomes the primary route to her birthplace.

If Elena does not appear in the national Burials index (collection 1520597, item 5), which is partial, browse image groups 004514823 and 004514824 (Barsebäck parish) from collection 1974200, which are browse-only (personCount 0) and cover from 1648 onward. The family lived in Barsebäck from at least September 1718 (son's christening) and son Asmund Jönsson died there in 1768, so Elena most likely died in Barsebäck as well. The original burial entry in the parish register may record her age at death and place of origin more fully than an index.

The loc_002 locality guide notes that household tax lists (mantalslängder) for the härad survive from 1658 and are held at Riksarkivet (National Archives of Sweden). Annual mantalslängder listed each taxable household head; some years' lists include all household members. Searching for a household headed by Asmund in Harjager härad from ~1690 to 1715 (up to Elena's marriage) would track his family's location year-by-year, confirm his presence in the härad, and — in years where all members are named — may list Elena as a resident daughter before her marriage. This is the required FAN/contextual item for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). It is placed last because it requires contact with or a visit to Riksarkivet and draws on the parish-level findings of earlier items to focus the search on the right härad and time window. Whose lifespan sets the window: Asmund's, as the household head whose records are sought.

items.rationale: Sweden, Baptisms, 1611-1920 (collection 1520594) is name-searchable with over 20 million persons. Elena married in December 1712 at an estimated age of 17-27, placing her birth circa 1685-1695. Her patronymic surname Asmundsdotter confirms her father was named Asmund. Search for Elena and all documented name variants — Elena = Helena = Ellen = Elin = Eljena, per the Sweden_Naming_Customs wiki page — with surname Asmundsdotter (also abbreviated d., dr., dtr.) in the Malmöhus area. A hit would directly supply her baptism date and her parents' names. Note: Västra Karaby's register begins 1688 (loc_002), so a birth before 1688 would leave no baptism entry in that parish's register; the national index draws from multiple parishes and may cover a nearby parish where an earlier entry survives.

The marriage of Elena Asmundsdotter and Jöns Jönsson on 29 December 1712 in Västra Karaby is recorded in the project tree as a fact with no source attached. The Västra Karaby church records (collection 1974200) are browse-only (personCount 0); image groups 004523021 and 004523018 cover this parish through 1804. Browsing the marriage register around December 1712 retrieves the original entry, which in Swedish Lutheran practice of this era routinely recorded the groom's and bride's fathers' names — the most direct potential source for naming Elena's parents. The image group 004523021 also covers Saxtorp parish in the same volumes, which may be relevant if Elena originated there.

Per Appendix B, a parentage plan requires a dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage. Elena's father was Asmund (from her patronymic); her mother's given name and maiden name are unknown. Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 (collection 1520596) is name-searchable with over 3.6 million persons. Search for a groom named Asmund in the Harjager härad or Malmöhus county area, circa 1675-1702. The date window is set to the plausible range for a couple whose daughter married in 1712 (parents' marriage approximately 15-37 years before the daughter's). This record would supply the mother's maiden name — unavailable from the patronymic — and confirm the parents as a couple. Note the limit: this record proves the couple married but does not by itself place Elena as their child; a record co-locating Elena with her parents (items 1, 4) is still required for a parentage conclusion.

Image group 004523018 covers Västra Karaby 1688-1804 and is browse-only (personCount 0), as part of collection 1974200. Swedish husförhörslängder (household examination rolls) organized each household and listed all members with their ages, updated across multiple years. Browsing pre-1712 rolls in Västra Karaby would show a household headed by Asmund and list Elena as a daughter still resident before her December 1712 marriage — directly placing her in her natal household and confirming parentage. The rolls may also record Elena's year of birth, corroborating or correcting the estimate from her marriage age. If Asmund's household is absent from Västra Karaby rolls, that narrows the parish of origin to elsewhere in the härad.

Elena's death date is unknown; she was demonstrably alive in September 1718 when her son was christened. Sweden, Burials, 1649-1920 (collection 1520597) is name-searchable with nearly 2.9 million persons. Search for Elena Asmundsdotter, or under her married household (wife of Jöns Jönsson) in Malmöhus county from 1718 onward. Swedish burial register entries of this era commonly recorded the deceased's age at death and home parish or place of origin — evidence that could supply her birthplace and narrow the birth-year window for the baptism search. This item is also required because Västra Karaby's register begins 1688 (loc_002), and Elena's birth may predate it: if no baptism entry survives, a burial entry stating her age or origin becomes the primary route to her birthplace.

If Elena does not appear in the national Burials index (collection 1520597, item 5), which is partial, browse image groups 004514823 and 004514824 (Barsebäck parish) from collection 1974200, which are browse-only (personCount 0) and cover from 1648 onward. The family lived in Barsebäck from at least September 1718 (son's christening) and son Asmund Jönsson died there in 1768, so Elena most likely died in Barsebäck as well. The original burial entry in the parish register may record her age at death and place of origin more fully than an index.

The loc_002 locality guide notes that household tax lists (mantalslängder) for the härad survive from 1658 and are held at Riksarkivet (National Archives of Sweden). Annual mantalslängder listed each taxable household head; some years' lists include all household members. Searching for a household headed by Asmund in Harjager härad from ~1690 to 1715 (up to Elena's marriage) would track his family's location year-by-year, confirm his presence in the härad, and — in years where all members are named — may list Elena as a resident daughter before her marriage. This is the required FAN/contextual item for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). It is placed last because it requires contact with or a visit to Riksarkivet and draws on the parish-level findings of earlier items to focus the search on the right härad and time window. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
